expectedText:
WILLIAMSON ACT (LAND CONSERVATION CONTRACT) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield · San Diego County

PURPOSE OF THIS DOCUMENT: THE WILLIAMSON ACT
This document concerns real property located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, in San Diego County County, California, identified by Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789 and described as Lot 12, Block 3, Tract No. 4567, as per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County Records, owned by Pat Morgan.

This document describes California's Land Conservation Act of 1965, commonly known as the Williamson Act (Government Code Section 51200 et seq.): a state law under which a city or county may enter into a contract with an agricultural or open-space landowner restricting the land to agricultural or open-space use in exchange for the land being valued, for property tax purposes, based on its restricted use rather than its unrestricted fair market value. It covers how a Williamson Act contract is formed and automatically renews, the notice-of-nonrenewal procedure that lets either party let a contract run out, the separate and more difficult cancellation procedure and its cancellation fee, and the income-capitalization method used to value enforceably restricted land for property tax purposes.

This document is distinct from this corpus's Subdivision Map Act document, which concerns the different process of dividing land into parcels, and from this corpus's Property Tax Parent-Child Transfer Exclusion (Proposition 19) document, which concerns a different property tax mechanism (a reassessment exclusion on an intra-family transfer) with no connection to a Williamson Act contract. It does not itself create, renew, give notice of nonrenewal for, or cancel any Williamson Act contract, and does not determine whether any specific parcel is eligible for, or currently subject to, such a contract; this is not a substitute for consulting the contracting city or county, the county assessor, or a licensed attorney about a specific parcel.

THE STATUTE'S NAME AND ITS CORE DEFINITIONS
California's Government Code states that the chapter establishing this framework "shall be known as the California Land Conservation Act of 1965 or as the Williamson Act." The same chapter defines an "agricultural preserve" as an area devoted to agricultural use, recreational use, or open-space use, or any combination of those uses, established in accordance with the chapter's own provisions, and defines "agricultural use" as the use of land, including greenhouses, for the purpose of producing an agricultural commodity for commercial purposes. A Williamson Act contract restricts land within an agricultural preserve to one or more of these defined uses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This chapter shall be known as the California Land Conservation Act of 1965 or as the Williamson Act."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51200, California Government Code, the chapter's popular name (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51200.)
  "“Agricultural preserve” means an area devoted to either agricultural use, as defined in subdivision (b), recreational use as defined in subdivision (n), or open-space use as defined in subdivision (o), or any combination of those uses and which is established in accordance with the provisions of this chapter."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51201(d), California Government Code, definition of "agricultural preserve", treated as one source with § 51201(b) below, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51201.)
  "“Agricultural use” means use of land, including but not limited to greenhouses, for the purpose of producing an agricultural commodity for commercial purposes."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51201(b), California Government Code, definition of "agricultural use", treated as one source with § 51201(d) above, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51201.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the chapter's own popular name and two of its statutory definitions; it does not evaluate whether any specific parcel in fact lies within an established agricultural preserve, or whether any specific use in fact qualifies as an "agricultural use," "recreational use," or "open-space use" as those terms are separately defined elsewhere in the same section — those are fact-specific determinations for the contracting city or county.

A CITY OR COUNTY'S AUTHORITY TO ENTER INTO A WILLIAMSON ACT CONTRACT
California's Government Code authorizes, but does not require, a city or county to contract with a landowner to limit the use of agricultural land for the purpose of preserving that land, subject to the conditions the contract itself states and the conditions this chapter states. The statute also permits a contract to include restrictions, terms, and conditions — including payments and fees — that are more restrictive than, or in addition to, what the chapter itself requires. A Williamson Act contract is accordingly a voluntary agreement between a landowner and a city or county, not a restriction the statute itself imposes on land directly.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any city or county may by contract limit the use of agricultural land for the purpose of preserving such land pursuant and subject to the conditions set forth in the contract and in this chapter. A contract may provide for restrictions, terms, and conditions, including payments and fees, more restrictive than or in addition to those required by this chapter."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51240, California Government Code, authority of a city or county to contract limiting agricultural land use (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51240.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the general contracting authority the statute grants; it does not evaluate whether any specific city or county has in fact established an agricultural preserve or elected to offer Williamson Act contracts, whether any specific parcel is eligible, or what additional restrictions, terms, or conditions a specific contract in fact contains — those are matters for the contracting city or county and the specific contract's own text.

MINIMUM CONTRACT TERM AND AUTOMATIC ANNUAL RENEWAL
California's Government Code requires that a Williamson Act contract be for an initial term of no less than 10 years. The statute then adds a self-renewing feature: each contract must provide that, on the contract's anniversary date or another annual date the contract specifies, a year is added automatically to the initial term, unless a party serves a notice of nonrenewal as the statute separately provides. As a result, a Williamson Act contract that no party ever moves to end continues to roll forward with a rolling term of approximately 10 years measured from whatever the current year happens to be, rather than expiring on a fixed date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Each contract shall be for an initial term of no less than 10 years. Each contract shall provide that on the anniversary date of the contract or such other annual date as specified by the contract a year shall be added automatically to the initial term unless notice of nonrenewal is given as provided in Section 51245."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51244(a), California Government Code, minimum contract term and automatic annual renewal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51244.)
  Known gap: This clause states the chapter's general 10-year minimum term and automatic-renewal rule. The same section contains additional, more detailed provisions — not quoted or summarized in this clause — governing a county's option to phase in a shortened 9-year or 18-year term under specified conditions tied to a county revenue determination, and exceptions to that phase-in for certain contract types; a landowner or county should consult the full text of Government Code Section 51244 for those details, which this document does not attempt to restate in full.

ENDING A CONTRACT BY NOTICE OF NONRENEWAL
California's Government Code lets either the landowner or the contracting city or county end the automatic-renewal cycle described elsewhere in this document by serving written notice of nonrenewal on the other party in advance of the contract's annual renewal date. The statute sets different minimum notice periods for each party: a landowner must serve notice at least 90 days before the renewal date, and a city or county must serve notice at least 60 days before the renewal date; a notice served later than that is not effective to prevent that year's automatic renewal. A landowner who receives a nonrenewal notice from the city or county may make a written protest of it, and the city or county may withdraw its own notice at any time before the renewal date. Once a party serves an effective notice of nonrenewal, the contract does not end immediately: because each earlier year's automatic renewal already added a year to the term, an effective notice of nonrenewal instead stops any further automatic renewal, so the existing contract term runs out on its own schedule, winding down year by year, rather than terminating on the notice's effective date. The statute also requires the clerk of the board or council to record a copy of the notice of nonrenewal, or of any withdrawal of that notice, with the county recorder within 20 days after the city or county receives, serves, or withdraws it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If either the landowner or the city or county desires in any year not to renew the contract, that party shall serve written notice of nonrenewal of the contract upon the other party in advance of the annual renewal date of the contract. Unless such written notice is served by the landowner at least 90 days prior to the renewal date or by the city or county at least 60 days prior to the renewal date, the contract shall be considered renewed as provided in Section 51244 or Section 51244.5."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51245, California Government Code, notice of nonrenewal procedure and minimum notice periods (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51245.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the general notice-of-nonrenewal procedure and its minimum notice periods; it does not evaluate whether a specific notice was in fact served within the statutory deadline, or state what remains of a specific contract's term at any given point, because that depends on the specific contract's own anniversary date and renewal history. The statute also permits a board or council, on the owner's request, to authorize a notice of nonrenewal covering only a portion of the land under contract — a partial-nonrenewal option this clause notes but does not further describe.

CANCELLATION: A SEPARATE, MORE DIFFICULT PROCESS THAN NONRENEWAL
Separately from letting a contract run out through nonrenewal, California's Government Code lets a landowner petition the contracting board or council to cancel a Williamson Act contract before its term ends, as to all or part of the land. The board or council may give tentative approval to cancel a contract only if it makes one of two required findings: that the cancellation is consistent with the chapter's purposes, or that the cancellation is in the public interest. For a finding that cancellation is consistent with the chapter's purposes, the statute requires the board or council to make a further set of findings, including that a notice of nonrenewal has already been served for the land, that the cancellation is not likely to cause adjacent land to leave agricultural use, that the proposed alternative use is consistent with the applicable general plan, that it will not result in discontiguous patterns of urban development, and that there is no proximate, suitable, noncontracted land available for the proposed alternative use (or that using the contracted land would create more contiguous development than using such other land). The statute separately states that the uneconomic character of an existing agricultural use is not, by itself, sufficient reason for cancellation, unless there is no other reasonable or comparable agricultural use to which the land may be put.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The landowner may petition the board or council for cancellation of any contract as to all or any part of the subject land. The board or council may grant tentative approval for cancellation of a contract only if it makes one of the following findings: (1) That the cancellation is consistent with the purposes of this chapter. (2) That cancellation is in the public interest."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51282(a), California Government Code, petition for cancellation and the two required findings, treated as one source with § 51282(b) and (d) below, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51282.)
  "That the cancellation is for land on which a notice of nonrenewal has been served pursuant to Section 51245. (2) That cancellation is not likely to result in the removal of adjacent lands from agricultural use. (3) That cancellation is for an alternative use which is consistent with the applicable provisions of the city or county general plan. (4) That cancellation will not result in discontiguous patterns of urban development."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51282(b), California Government Code, findings required for a "consistent with purposes" cancellation, treated as one source with § 51282(a) and (d), not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51282.)
  "For purposes of subdivision (a), the uneconomic character of an existing agricultural use shall not by itself be sufficient reason for cancellation of the contract. The uneconomic character of the existing use may be considered only if there is no other reasonable or comparable agricultural use to which the land may be put."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51282(d), California Government Code, uneconomic character of existing use is not by itself sufficient, treated as one source with § 51282(a) and (b) above, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51282.)
  Known gap: This clause states the chapter's own required findings for cancellation; it does not evaluate whether any of those findings would in fact be made for a specific parcel, which the statute commits to the contracting board or council after notice and hearing on a specific petition and a specific proposed alternative use, not to any generalized fact stated in this document. The statute's alternative "public interest" finding, and further procedural requirements for the landowner's petition and proposed alternative use, are addressed only in part in this clause.

THE CANCELLATION FEE: VALUATION AND THE 12.5% RATE
Before giving tentative approval to cancel a contract, California's Government Code requires the county assessor to determine the land's current fair market value as though it were free of the contractual restriction, and to certify that "cancellation valuation" to the board or council for the purpose of calculating the cancellation fee. The board or council must then determine and certify to the county auditor the cancellation fee the landowner is to pay the county treasurer upon cancellation, which the statute sets at an amount equal to 12.5 percent of that cancellation valuation. The statute separately states the Legislature's intent that this fee is not a tax, but a payment that, when made, confers a private benefit tending to increase the value of the property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Prior to any action by the board or council giving tentative approval to the cancellation of any contract, the county assessor of the county in which the land is located shall determine the current fair market value of the land as though it were free of the contractual restriction."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51283(a), California Government Code, assessor's fair-market-value determination for the cancellation fee, treated as one source with § 51283(b) and (f) below, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51283.)
  "Prior to giving tentative approval to the cancellation of any contract, the board or council shall determine and certify to the county auditor the amount of the cancellation fee that the landowner shall pay the county treasurer upon cancellation. That fee shall be an amount equal to 12 1 / 2 percent of the cancellation valuation of the property."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51283(b), California Government Code, the 12.5% cancellation fee rate, treated as one source with § 51283(a) and (f), not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51283.)
  "It is the intent of the Legislature that fees paid to cancel a contract do not constitute taxes but are payments that, when made, provide a private benefit that tends to increase the value of the property."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51283(f), California Government Code, legislative intent that the cancellation fee is not a tax, treated as one source with § 51283(a) and (b) above, not an independent source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51283.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general valuation and fee-rate rule; it does not restate the statute's separate provisions letting a board or council waive or defer all or part of the fee, in the public interest and with the state Secretary of the Natural Resources Agency's approval, where cancellation results from an involuntary transfer or change in permitted land use and other conditions are met — a discretionary exception this clause notes but does not evaluate for any specific parcel.

CERTIFICATE OF TENTATIVE CANCELLATION AND THE LANDOWNER'S CONDITIONS
California's Government Code describes the recorded paper trail that follows tentative approval of a cancellation petition accompanied by a specified alternative-use proposal. The clerk of the board or council must record, with the county recorder, a certificate of tentative cancellation stating the landowner's name, that a certificate of cancellation will be issued and recorded once specified conditions and contingencies are satisfied, a description of those conditions and contingencies, and a legal description of the property. Payment in full of the cancellation fee is one required condition, and the statute warns that if the fee is not paid, or a certificate of cancellation is not issued, within one year from the assessor's valuation date, the fee is subject to recomputation. The statute also requires the landowner to obtain all permits necessary to commence the proposed alternative-use project as one of the conditions to be satisfied.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Upon tentative approval of a petition accompanied by a proposal for a specified alternative use of the land, the clerk of the board or council shall record in the office of the county recorder of the county in which is located the land as to which the contract is applicable a certificate of tentative cancellation, which shall set forth the name of the landowner requesting the cancellation, the fact that a certificate of cancellation of contract will be issued and recorded at the time that specified conditions and contingencies are satisfied, a description of the conditions and contingencies which must be satisfied, and a legal description of the property."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51283.4(a), California Government Code, recorded certificate of tentative cancellation and its required content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51283.4.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general certificate-of-tentative-cancellation procedure; it does not restate the statute's separate provisions on a landowner's right to request an earlier recomputation of the valuation, or on the certificate-of-withdrawal procedure that applies if the landowner is unable to satisfy the stated conditions and contingencies (under which, the statute states, the landowner is not entitled to a refund of any cancellation fee already paid) — both addressed in the same section but not quoted in this clause.

JUDICIAL REVIEW OF A CANCELLATION DECISION
California's Government Code channels any challenge to a board of supervisors' or city council's decision to cancel a Williamson Act contract, on the ground of alleged noncompliance with the chapter's requirements, into a specific procedure: such an action or proceeding must be brought under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1094.5, the state's general statute for judicial review of a local agency's adjudicatory decision. The statute also sets a short limitations period: the action or proceeding must be commenced within 180 days of the date of the council's or board's order acting on the cancellation petition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any action or proceeding which, on the grounds of alleged noncompliance with the requirements of this chapter, seeks to attack, review, set aside, void, or annul a decision of a board of supervisors or a city council to cancel a contract shall be brought pursuant to Section 1094.5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (b) The action or proceeding shall be commenced within 180 days from the date of the council or board order acting on a petition for cancellation filed under this chapter."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 51286, California Government Code, judicial review procedure and 180-day limitations period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=51286.)
  Known gap: This clause states the chapter's own procedural vehicle and limitations period for challenging a cancellation decision; it does not describe the substantive standard of review a court applies under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1094.5 itself, which was not separately fetched or cited in this document, and does not evaluate whether any specific challenge would in fact be timely or meritorious.

PROPERTY TAX VALUATION: CAPITALIZED INCOME, NOT FAIR MARKET VALUE
California's Revenue and Taxation Code states the property tax valuation method that makes a Williamson Act contract financially significant to a landowner. Rather than the sales-comparison approach ordinarily used to value real property, when valuing enforceably restricted open-space land the county assessor is directed not to consider sales data on land (restricted or not), and instead to value the land by the capitalization-of-income method the statute describes. The statute directs that, where sufficient rental information is available, the income capitalized is the fair rent imputed to the land based on actual and typical rentals for similar land in similar use where the owner pays the property tax; where sufficient rental information is not available, the income is what the land can reasonably be expected to yield under prudent management, subject to the applicable enforceable restriction. It is this substitution of a capitalized-income valuation for a fair-market-value valuation, while a contract remains in force, that typically produces a lower assessed value and lower property tax bill than the same land would carry if unrestricted.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Except as provided in Sections 423.7 and 423.8, when valuing enforceably restricted open-space land, other than land used for the production of timber for commercial purposes, the county assessor shall not consider sales data on lands, whether or not enforceably restricted, but shall value these lands by the capitalization of income method"
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 423, California Revenue and Taxation Code, capitalization-of-income valuation method for enforceably restricted open-space land (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=423.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general capitalization-of-income valuation rule; it does not restate the statute's own listed exceptions (land used for commercial timber production, and land addressed by Revenue and Taxation Code Sections 423.7 and 423.8, neither of which was separately fetched or cited in this document), and does not calculate or estimate what assessed value or tax bill would in fact result for any specific parcel, which depends on rent and income data this document does not have.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF REVIEW
By signing below, Pat Morgan acknowledges having reviewed this information sheet describing the Williamson Act's contract, nonrenewal, cancellation, and property tax valuation provisions as they existed on the date checked in this document, with respect to the property at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, San Diego County County, California.

This document is informational only. It does not create, modify, renew, give notice of nonrenewal for, or cancel any Williamson Act contract, and it is not a substitute for reviewing the specific contract recorded against this property, contacting the contracting city or county and the county assessor, or consulting a licensed attorney about this property's specific circumstances.

Signature of Pat Morgan: _________________________ Date: September 1, 2026

citations.quote: That the cancellation is for land on which a notice of nonrenewal has been served pursuant to Section 51245. (2) That cancellation is not likely to result in the removal of adjacent lands from agricultural use. (3) That cancellation is for an alternative use which is consistent with the applicable provisions of the city or county general plan. (4) That cancellation will not result in discontiguous patterns of urban development.

citations.cite: California Government Code, uneconomic character of existing use is not by itself sufficient, treated as one source with § 51282(a) and (b) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: For purposes of subdivision (a), the uneconomic character of an existing agricultural use shall not by itself be sufficient reason for cancellation of the contract. The uneconomic character of the existing use may be considered only if there is no other reasonable or comparable agricultural use to which the land may be put.

The statute's alternative "public interest" finding, and further procedural requirements for the landowner's petition and proposed alternative use, are addressed only in part in this clause.

expectedJSON.body: Before giving tentative approval to cancel a contract, California's Government Code requires the county assessor to determine the land's current fair market value as though it were free of the contractual restriction, and to certify that "cancellation valuation" to the board or council for the purpose of calculating the cancellation fee. The board or council must then determine and certify to the county auditor the cancellation fee the landowner is to pay the county treasurer upon cancellation, which the statute sets at an amount equal to 12.5 percent of that cancellation valuation. The statute separately states the Legislature's intent that this fee is not a tax, but a payment that, when made, confers a private benefit tending to increase the value of the property.

citations.cite: California Government Code, assessor's fair-market-value determination for the cancellation fee, treated as one source with § 51283(b) and (f) below, not an independent source
citations.quote: Prior to any action by the board or council giving tentative approval to the cancellation of any contract, the county assessor of the county in which the land is located shall determine the current fair market value of the land as though it were free of the contractual restriction.

citations.cite: California Government Code, the 12.5% cancellation fee rate, treated as one source with § 51283(a) and (f), not an independent source
citations.quote: Prior to giving tentative approval to the cancellation of any contract, the board or council shall determine and certify to the county auditor the amount of the cancellation fee that the landowner shall pay the county treasurer upon cancellation. That fee shall be an amount equal to 12 1 / 2 percent of the cancellation valuation of the property.

citations.cite: California Government Code, legislative intent that the cancellation fee is not a tax, treated as one source with § 51283(a) and (b) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature that fees paid to cancel a contract do not constitute taxes but are payments that, when made, provide a private benefit that tends to increase the value of the property.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the general valuation and fee-rate rule; it does not restate the statute's separate provisions letting a board or council waive or defer all or part of the fee, in the public interest and with the state Secretary of the Natural Resources Agency's approval, where cancellation results from an involuntary transfer or change in permitted land use and other conditions are met — a discretionary exception this clause notes but does not evaluate for any specific parcel.

expectedJSON.body: California's Government Code describes the recorded paper trail that follows tentative approval of a cancellation petition accompanied by a specified alternative-use proposal. The clerk of the board or council must record, with the county recorder, a certificate of tentative cancellation stating the landowner's name, that a certificate of cancellation will be issued and recorded once specified conditions and contingencies are satisfied, a description of those conditions and contingencies, and a legal description of the property. Payment in full of the cancellation fee is one required condition, and the statute warns that if the fee is not paid, or a certificate of cancellation is not issued, within one year from the assessor's valuation date, the fee is subject to recomputation. The statute also requires the landowner to obtain all permits necessary to commence the proposed alternative-use project as one of the conditions to be satisfied.

citations.cite: California Government Code, recorded certificate of tentative cancellation and its required content
citations.quote: Upon tentative approval of a petition accompanied by a proposal for a specified alternative use of the land, the clerk of the board or council shall record in the office of the county recorder of the county in which is located the land as to which the contract is applicable a certificate of tentative cancellation, which shall set forth the name of the landowner requesting the cancellation, the fact that a certificate of cancellation of contract will be issued and recorded at the time that specified conditions and contingencies are satisfied, a description of the conditions and contingencies which must be satisfied, and a legal description of the property.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the general certificate-of-tentative-cancellation procedure; it does not restate the statute's separate provisions on a landowner's right to request an earlier recomputation of the valuation, or on the certificate-of-withdrawal procedure that applies if the landowner is unable to satisfy the stated conditions and contingencies (under which, the statute states, the landowner is not entitled to a refund of any cancellation fee already paid) — both addressed in the same section but not quoted in this clause.

expectedJSON.body: California's Government Code channels any challenge to a board of supervisors' or city council's decision to cancel a Williamson Act contract, on the ground of alleged noncompliance with the chapter's requirements, into a specific procedure: such an action or proceeding must be brought under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1094.5, the state's general statute for judicial review of a local agency's adjudicatory decision. The statute also sets a short limitations period: the action or proceeding must be commenced within 180 days of the date of the council's or board's order acting on the cancellation petition.

citations.cite: California Government Code, judicial review procedure and 180-day limitations period
citations.quote: Any action or proceeding which, on the grounds of alleged noncompliance with the requirements of this chapter, seeks to attack, review, set aside, void, or annul a decision of a board of supervisors or a city council to cancel a contract shall be brought pursuant to Section 1094.5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (b) The action or proceeding shall be commenced within 180 days from the date of the council or board order acting on a petition for cancellation filed under this chapter.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the chapter's own procedural vehicle and limitations period for challenging a cancellation decision; it does not describe the substantive standard of review a court applies under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1094.5 itself, which was not separately fetched or cited in this document, and does not evaluate whether any specific challenge would in fact be timely or meritorious.

expectedJSON.body: California's Revenue and Taxation Code states the property tax valuation method that makes a Williamson Act contract financially significant to a landowner. Rather than the sales-comparison approach ordinarily used to value real property, when valuing enforceably restricted open-space land the county assessor is directed not to consider sales data on land (restricted or not), and instead to value the land by the capitalization-of-income method the statute describes. The statute directs that, where sufficient rental information is available, the income capitalized is the fair rent imputed to the land based on actual and typical rentals for similar land in similar use where the owner pays the property tax; where sufficient rental information is not available, the income is what the land can reasonably be expected to yield under prudent management, subject to the applicable enforceable restriction. It is this substitution of a capitalized-income valuation for a fair-market-value valuation, while a contract remains in force, that typically produces a lower assessed value and lower property tax bill than the same land would carry if unrestricted.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, capitalization-of-income valuation method for enforceably restricted open-space land
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 423.7 and 423.8, when valuing enforceably restricted open-space land, other than land used for the production of timber for commercial purposes, the county assessor shall not consider sales data on lands, whether or not enforceably restricted, but shall value these lands by the capitalization of income method

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the general capitalization-of-income valuation rule; it does not restate the statute's own listed exceptions (land used for commercial timber production, and land addressed by Revenue and Taxation Code Sections 423.7 and 423.8, neither of which was separately fetched or cited in this document), and does not calculate or estimate what assessed value or tax bill would in fact result for any specific parcel, which depends on rent and income data this document does not have.
